item.title: Asteroid 2018 EH4 passes by
item.description:
14.10.2026, 05:49 UTC

An asteroid with an estimated diameter of 123–275 m will pass Earth at 8.43 million km, or 21.9 times the Earth–Moon distance, travelling at 13.2 km/s. For scale: roughly the size of a small hill. This is not a close encounter – it makes the list as one of the largest objects passing us this week. NASA classifies it as “potentially hazardous” – but that is purely a technical category for objects larger than about 140 m whose orbits come close to Earth's. No known object threatens us in the foreseeable future.

Object record in the JPL database

Upcoming close approaches – CNEOS

item.title: New Glenn | Blue Ring-1
item.description:
31.12.2026, 00:00 UTC

Launch of New Glenn, operated by Blue Origin. Site: Cape Canaveral SFS, FL, USA. Schedule status: date to be determined. Mission: The first mission of Blue Ring, Blue Origin's all-in-one, high-powered hybrid solar electric and chemical propelled spacecraft, will test the spacecraft's operations in Geostationary Transfer Orbit (GTO), as well as subsequent operations after reaching Geostationary Orbit (GEO). It will carry one of Scout Space's flagship next-generation space domain awareness (SDA) Owl sensors, which is designed to enhance real-time tracking, characterization, and assessment of space objects by integrating advanced optical sensing, onboard artificial intelligence-driven processing, and autonomous decision-making capabilities to deliver domain-wide intelligence in space in support of the U.S. Space Force’s space control mission set. Blue Ring will also carry Optimum Technologies (OpTech)'s next-generation Caracal optical payload, which is designed to provide actionable insights on resident space objects and orbital activity and includes onboard image storage, object detection algorithms, and passive thermal control. The payload is designed to operate flexibly across dynamic orbits over a year-long mission profile. Several internal Blue Origin payloads will also be hosted. Launch dates slip often – check the current status before tuning into a webcast.

item.title: Southern Taurids meteor shower peak
item.description:
05.11.2027, 02:00 UTC

Few meteors, but an unusual share of fireballs – slow, very bright and worth the wait. At maximum, up to 5 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Taurus. A Moon 38% illuminated will brighten the sky a little. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

item.title: Orionids meteor shower peak
item.description:
21.10.2027, 02:00 UTC

The year's second helping of dust from Halley's Comet, with fast, bright meteors. At maximum, up to 20 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Orion. Unfortunately the Moon will be 68% illuminated and will drown out the fainter meteors – it is worth observing after it sets. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.

item.title: Draconids meteor shower peak
item.description:
08.10.2027, 02:00 UTC

An unpredictable shower: usually weak, but a few times in history it has produced genuine meteor storms. The radiant is already high in the early evening. At maximum, up to 10 meteors per hour in theory (the ZHR – under a perfectly dark sky with the radiant overhead; in practice usually several times fewer). The radiant lies in Draco. A Moon 56% illuminated will brighten the sky a little. No equipment needed – just a reclining chair, warm clothes and a spot away from city lights.
